back: A unique identifier given to a device's NIC at manufacture, used to identify the device on a network.
48 bits, written as 12 hex digits in six pairs: first half manufacturer code, second half serial number.
An address allocated to a device by the network it joins, used to identify it and route data to it across networks.

front: Static compared with dynamic IP address?
back: Static: permanently assigned, never changes (servers, printers). Dynamic: assigned each time a device connects, may change.
32 bits, four denary numbers from 0 to 255 separated by full stops, e.g. 10.4.8.200.
128 bits, eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons; leading zeros and one run of zero groups (::) can be omitted.
IPv4 gives only about 4.3 billion addresses, too few for all connected devices; IPv6 gives vastly more.

front: Why can't an IPv4 number be 300?
back: Each number is 8 bits, so the largest value is 255.

front: Which address changes when a laptop moves to a new network?
back: The IP address (allocated by each network); the MAC address stays the same.
